newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Big dollar rise gets Swiss bourse's blessings.
newsitem.headline: Big dollar rise gets Swiss bourse's blessings.

text.p: Bourse traders hope the latest dollar rise will fuel further gains in Swiss shares, while Switzerland's multinationals see the dollar's strength as likely to boost currency-related profits if the trend continues.

The Swiss franc hit its lowest levels versus the dollar in nearly four years on Friday. The dollar was also sharply higher against the German mark, which posted its lowest levels versus the U.S. unit in nearly six years.
"I would say we have a generally positive background for the share market," said one Swiss bourse trader, adding part of this was due to the dollar.
"The dollar has clearly helped. For many companies it is very positive," the share dealer said.
The dollar breached 1.51 Swiss francs on Friday, getting as high as 1.5176, its highest level against the Swiss currency since August 1993.

The dollar may also revive the Swiss Market Index of blue-chip stocks, which set an all-time high on July 9 of 6,101.2 and then fell back. The SMI traded on Friday afternoon nearly unchanged from Thursday's close of 5,849.2.

A stronger dollar, providing it is not already factored into prices, should still benefit shares of many big Swiss firms, traders said. These include cement and construction giant Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG and pharmaceutical firms Novartis AG and Roche Holding AG. Zurich Group, the Swiss insurer which recently bought U.S. investment house Scudder, Stevens & Clark, was also seen favoured by a firm dollar, traders said.

The dollar factor is seen as important for Swiss exports. The U.S. has surpassed France this year to become Switzerland's second-biggest export market, with over nine percent of the total. Some other countries import goods on a dollar-related basis.
The strong dollar was frosting on what has been a generally favourable year already at some firms.
"For us it is positive," said Hans-Caspar Ryser, spokesman for Sulzer AG.

The dollar strength was especially favourable for Sulzer's production in Switzerland of weaving machines and compressors. Much of such equipment is exported to countries with exports based on dollars, Ryser said.
Nestle AG, headquartered in Switzerland but with much of its sales abroad, also is watching the dollar trend.

"It is obvious, it goes without saying, since we do almost half of our business in dollar or dollar-related currencies, the dollar is most important to us. Every dollar (move) up and down therefore affects us," said a spokesman for Nestle.

For the overall Swiss economy, Germany is still the main export market, accounting for roughly a quarter of Swiss exports. Dollar gains also helped to offset worries about a drop in the mark to an 11-month low versus the Swiss franc earlier this week, which would bode poorly for Swiss exports.

The mark's sharp drop versus the dollar may however also be indirectly positive for Switzerland if it helps German exports. Share traders reason that a pick-up in demand for German goods should eventually stimulate German demand for Swiss goods.
The Swiss National Bank (SNB), meanwhile, is unlikely to stand in the way of a further dollar/Swiss rise.

In the past year it has been prompt to add liquidity to the Swiss money market in times when it perceived the franc as overvalued but has not seemed worried about any franc weakness, which could be inflationary. The economy has been slow enough to make exports the main priority. The latest currency moves are also seen based on thin volume, and may be exaggerated.
"We have the impression that the market is very thin, and in such cases volatility is not unusual," said an SNB spokesman in response to an inquiry.
